closing.translation: Om. My speech is established in my mind; my mind is established in my speech. O manifest one, be manifest to me. You two are the linch-pins of the Veda for me. May what I have heard not forsake me. By this that I have studied I join days and nights. I shall speak what is right; I shall speak what is true. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. May it protect me, may it protect the speaker, may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
notes: The peace invocation of the Upaniṣads of the Ṛgveda, printed at the opening of the e-text. Śaṅkara's Aitareya bhāṣya does not comment on it; the translation gives the plain sense of the words. ‘You two’ are speech and mind; ‘the speaker’ is the teacher. The e-text prints āṇīsthaḥ as one word.

translations.text: ‘Who is this whom we worship as the Self? Which of the two is that Self?’ (Is it) that by which one sees, or by which one hears, or by which one smells odours, or by which one utters speech, or by which one knows the sweet and the not sweet?

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the adhyāya: the gaining of the fruit, to be the Self of all, which the means, the knowledge of Brahman, brings about, is made known by the śruti through the line of teachers, Vāmadeva and the rest, and is very well known in the assembly of the knowers of Brahman. Perceiving this, the brāhmaṇas of today who seek liberation and wish to know Brahman, who wish to turn away from saṃsāra, which is non-eternal and consists of ends and means, up to and including the state of the jīva, reflect and ask one another: who is this Self?

Śaṅkara: the Self whom we worship directly as ‘this Self’, who is he? Him whom Vāmadeva worshipped directly as ‘this Self’ and so became immortal, him we too worship; who then is he? As they asked one another so, there arose a memory, born of the impression of what they had heard before of the particulars: ‘Brahman entered this Puruṣa by the tips of the feet’, and ‘having cleft this very parting he entered by this door’. Here two Brahmans have entered from opposite sides, and both are selves of this lump; one of the two must be the Self to be worshipped. Which is it? So they asked one another again, to settle the particular. As they reflected, this thought arose: two things are perceived in this lump, the instrument, divided in many ways, by which one perceives, and the one who perceives, who is one because he recalls and connects the objects perceived through the different organs. Of these, that by which one perceives cannot be the Self. By what does one perceive? By that which, as the eye, sees form; as the ear, hears sound; as the organ of smell, smells odours; as the organ of speech, utters speech that consists of names, ‘cow’, ‘horse’ and the like, and ‘good’ and ‘bad’; as the tongue, knows the sweet and the not sweet.
The e-text prints a daṇḍa after ko 'yam, removed here, and reads gandhāñ jighrati; Śaṅkara glosses gandhān ājighrati.

translations.text: That which is this heart, and this mind: awareness, lordship, understanding, consciousness, retentiveness, perception, firmness, thought, mastery of thought, distress, memory, conception, resolve, the working of life, desire, longing: all these are indeed names of consciousness.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: what, then, is that one instrument, divided in many ways?

Śaṅkara: what was told before, ‘the heart is the seed of creatures, the mind is the seed of the heart; by the mind the waters and Varuṇa were created’, and ‘from the heart the mind, from the mind the moon’, that same is this heart and mind: it is one, in many ways. By this one inner organ, as the eye, one sees form; as the ear, one hears; as the organ of smell, one smells; as speech, one speaks; as the tongue, one tastes; in its own form as the mind, which deliberates, one deliberates; in its form as the heart, one determines. So this one instrument, at work on the objects of all the organs, serves the perceiver for all perception: ‘having mounted speech by consciousness, one obtains all names by speech; having mounted the eye by consciousness, one obtains all forms by the eye’ (Kauṣītaki 3), ‘by the mind alone one sees, by the mind one hears; by the heart one knows forms’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.5.3). And prāṇa is of the same nature: ‘what is prāṇa is consciousness, what is consciousness is prāṇa’ (Kauṣītaki 3); prāṇa, we have said, is the aggregate of the organs. Therefore that Brahman which entered by the feet, being subordinate, the perceiver's instrument of perception, cannot be the Brahman that is the Self to be worshipped. What remains is the perceiver, for whose perception the workings of this instrument, the heart in the form of the mind, exist: he must be the Self we are to worship. So they concluded.

Śaṅkara: the workings of the inner organ, turned on outer and inner objects, which serve the perception of the perceiver, Brahman of the nature of consciousness dwelling in the adjunct of the inner organ, are now named. saṃjñāna is being aware, the state of being conscious; ājñāna is commanding, lordship; vijñāna is the knowledge of the arts and the like; prajñāna is being conscious; medhā is the power to retain texts; dṛṣṭi is the perception of all objects through the senses; dhṛti is the holding by which the body and senses are held up when they sink (‘by firmness they bear up the body’); mati is thinking; manīṣā is independence in it; jūti is the mind's state of being pained by sickness and the like; smṛti is remembering; saṅkalpa is the forming of colour and the rest as white, black and so on; kratu is determination; asu is the working that causes the act of living, breathing and the rest; kāma is the craving for an object that is not present, thirst; vaśa is the longing for union with women and the like. These and other workings of the inner organ serve the perception of the perceiver, who is consciousness alone; they are adjuncts of Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, and so become names of it, born of those adjuncts. All these are names of consciousness, not of itself directly: as it is said, ‘when breathing he comes to be called breath’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.7).

translations.text: This is Brahmā; this is Indra; this is Prajāpati; (this is) all these gods; and these five great elements, earth, air, space, water and light; and these (creatures) mixed with the small, the seeds of one kind and of another: those born of eggs, those born of wombs, those born of sweat and those born of sprouts; horses, cattle, men, elephants; whatever living thing there is here, that walks and that flies, and what is unmoving. All that is led by consciousness; it is established in consciousness. The world is led by consciousness; consciousness is its support. Consciousness is Brahman.

notes: Śaṅkara: this Self whose nature is consciousness is the lower Brahman, the prāṇa that is in all bodies, the self of consciousness: Hiraṇyagarbha, who has entered the adjuncts that are the inner organs like the reflections of the sun in different waters. He is Indra, by his quality or as king of the gods; he is Prajāpati, the first-born embodied one from whom fire and the other guardians were born through the bursting forth of the mouth and the rest; he is all these gods, fire and the rest. The five great elements, earth and the rest, are the material of all bodies, in the form of food and eater of food. ‘Mixed with the small’: together with the small creatures, snakes and the like (iva has no meaning here). ‘Seeds’ are causes, named in two groups, ‘of one kind and of another’: the egg-born, birds and the like; the womb-born, men and the like; the sweat-born, lice and the like; the sprout-born, trees and the like. ‘That walks’ is what moves on feet, ‘that flies’ what moves through the sky, ‘unmoving’ what does not move. All that is he alone.

Śaṅkara: ‘led by consciousness’: prajñā is consciousness, and that is Brahman; netra is that by which one is led; that which has consciousness for its leader is prajñā-netra. ‘Established in consciousness’: resting on Brahman at the times of its origin, continuance and dissolution. ‘The world is led by consciousness’, as before; or the whole world has consciousness for its eye. Consciousness is the support of the whole world; therefore consciousness is Brahman. This Brahman, with every distinction of adjunct gone, is spotless, stainless, actionless, at peace, one, without a second, to be known by the setting aside of every particular, ‘not this, not this’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.26), beyond the reach of all words and ideas. By connection with the adjunct of utterly pure consciousness it is the all-knowing Lord, who sets in motion the unmanifest seed of the world common to all, and as the controller is called the Inner Ruler. The same, identifying itself with the intellect that is the seed of the manifest world, is called Hiraṇyagarbha. The same, having for its adjunct the first body that arose within the egg, is called Virāj, Prajāpati. With the adjuncts of fire and the rest that arose from that, it is called a deity. So too in the particular bodies, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, Brahman takes this and that name and form. That one, divided by all its adjuncts, is known in every way by all creatures and by the logicians and imagined in many ways: ‘some call him Agni, others Manu, Prajāpati, some Indra, others prāṇa, others the eternal Brahman’ (Manu 12.123).

lines.iast: sa etena prajñenātmanāsmāl lokād utkramyāmuṣmin svarge loke sarvān kāmān āptvāmṛtaḥ samabhavat samabhavat

padaccheda.iast: saḥ etena prajñena ātmanā asmāt lokāt utkramya amuṣmin svarge loke sarvān kāmān āptvā amṛtaḥ samabhavat samabhavat
padaccheda.deva: सः एतेन प्रज्ञेन आत्मना अस्मात् लोकात् उत्क्रम्य अमुष्मिन् स्वर्गे लोके सर्वान् कामान् आप्त्वा अमृतः समभवत् समभवत्

translations.text: He (Vāmadeva, or another who knows Brahman thus), by this Self that is consciousness, having risen up from this world, having obtained all desires, became immortal in that heavenly world; he became immortal.

notes: Śaṅkara: Vāmadeva, or another who knows Brahman as it has been described. By that very Self that is consciousness by which the knowers of old became immortal, this knower too, having risen from this world, becomes immortal; the rest has been explained (on 2.1.6).
